newsitem.title: GERMANY: Scientists report breakthrough in fight against TB.
newsitem.headline: Scientists report breakthrough in fight against TB.

text.p: The World Health Organisation (WHO) said on Wednesday its new strategy for treating tuberculosis represented a breakthrough in tackling the age-old disease and could save millions of lives worldwide.

The WHO programme could also dramatically reduce the threat of the emergence of TB bacilli resistant to drugs and cut long-term costs, representatives from the United Nations health agency told a news conference in Berlin.
The plan, known as DOTS or Directly Observed Treatment Short-course, was causing the worldwide TB epidemic to level off for the first time in decades, they said.

It calls for training health workers or community members to counsel and observe TB patients to insure they take the standard four antibiotics, not only until symptoms disappear but until they are cured.

"This is the single most important development in the fight against humanity's oldest and most deadly disease since (German scientist) Robert Koch discovered the TB bacillus in 1882," the WHO's TB programme director, Arata Kochi, said.

"For the first time, we have the means to reverse the TB epidemic not only in wealthy countries, but in the world's poorest countries as well," Kochi said, adding that field research showed DOTS could double the chances of recovery.
WHO Director-General Hiroshi Nakajima said in a statement released in Geneva that DOTS was "the biggest health breakthrough of this decade, in terms of the lives we will be able to save".
He added: "We anticipate that at least 10 million deaths from tuberculosis will be prevented in the next 10 years with the introduction and extensive use of the DOTS strategy."
Programme Deputy Director Richard Bumgarner said DOTS could reduce costs in the developing world to less than $100 per patient for an entire course of treatment.
"This is a shift from having to hospitalise patients to treating people where they live," Bumgarner said. "That saves huge amounts of money."

"The usual treatment methods completely backfired because patients tend to stop taking their medication when they feel better," Kochi said. This allows the still-active bacilli to mutate and resist existing drugs.
"DOTS also dramatically reduces the threat of multi-drug resistant TB and can save millions of lives in the next decade," Kochi added.

Development and testing of the strategy had been going on for the past decade and had been spearheaded by a team from the WHO and researchers from five non-governmental organisations based in Europe and Japan.

Kochi said nearly three million people died from the disease last year, more people than at the epidemic's height in the first part of the century, when it swept across North America and Europe, killing one out of every seven people.

Although the TB was almost eliminated in Europe, Japan and North America, it had substantially increased in the rest of the world. And it has been making a comeback in parts of Europe and the United States.
"Without DOTS, in the next 10 years we expect another 80 million people to be infected, which is almost the entire population of Germany," Kochi said. "Of those 30 million are expected to die.

"But if 70 percent of those cases receive DOTS, the number of TB cases will decrease by half." He added that more than 70 countries, including Bangladesh, Peru and China, were already using DOTS with great success.
